title: Lake Agawam
summary: Lake Agawam is the modern Southampton pond connected with the Agawom or Agawam entry. The broader application of Agawam to Southampton is presented as a historical error rather than a secure local Indigenous placename. The more specific place is the town pond in Southampton Village, while earlier writers mistakenly applied Agawam to the whole town.
why_this_matters: Lake Agawam matters because it shows how careful place-name work can correct inherited mistakes while still honoring the Southampton landscape. William Wallace Tooker connected Agawam to the town pond but also warned that earlier writers had wrongly stretched the name across all of Southampton through confusion with Agawom in Massachusetts. That correction shows that Indigenous mapping is not only about preserving names, but also about reading sources carefully, respecting uncertainty, and not forcing a name where the evidence does not support it.
history_content: The name does not appear as a secure early Southampton-wide placename. The broader Southampton usage comes from a seventeenth-century confusion with Agawom in Massachusetts, making the history useful as a correction as much as a placename.
translation_content:
Agawom and Agawam have been interpreted, if a missing ending is supplied, as a place of going under or low flat meadows that are overflowed. That reading is tied to a correction of earlier scholarship and remains tentative.

Why Place Names Matter

“People’s knowledge of those landscapes, and the stories that are layered over it, are inscribed in the very words used to name the places.”

— Karen K. Gaul, Nanutset ch’u Q’udi Gu: Before Our Time and Now—An Ethnohistory of Lake Clark National Park and Preserve (2007), Maps and Place Names, printed p. 84
whereintheworld_content: Lake Agawam shows why placename work must preserve corrections as well as names. Mapping the pond helps identify the modern place, while keeping clear that Agawam is not a secure Shinnecock or Southampton-wide Indigenous name.
